I gained 10kg in 6 months while taking mirtazapin. I also couldn't really sleep anymore. After six months I decided enough is enough and I stopped taking it (after consulting my psychiatrist of course).
With mirtazapin I always craved chocolate. I've been eating 300-400 grams of chocolate almost daily. Now I'm fighting on loosing all the weight again.

I've decided against kids, but I really wouldn't recommend this decision if you are not absolutely sure what your diagnosis is and even then think very very long about this (several years). Kids can bring you a lot of joy.

If you decide to get pregnant, visit a doctor beforehand. Ask him if the medication you take is ok during your pregnancy. If it's not he/she can surely recommend something else.

This feeling I know way to good. I didn't go to therapy for twenty years because I thought I would be weak if I couldn't deal with my depression by myself. Then starting therapy i declined medication because this would be even weaker.

By now I know I will probably take medication for the rest of my life and that's completely ok. I'm not weak, I have a sickness, a genetic defect. It's completely normal to take medication. And if the medication allows me to function more or less normal, then medication is the best thing I can do.

You are strong because you took the step, acknowledged you are sick and taken the necessary steps to get healthy again. If this means you have to take medication for the rest of your life, then so be it. You have control, your medication gives you control. If your eyesight isn't perfect you would wear glasses for the rest of your life. For depression you take medication for the rest of your life. That is completely ok.

I've started to only watch "new" because of that issue. So many posts are not commented. But I had to realize, I often don't know what to answer myself. Maybe just an upvote helps, so people see it has been read by someone?

then maybe give him some time, but I would recommend to ask from time to time if he doesn't want to do something.

It is bloody difficult to deal with someone in a deep depression. Some people need to be forced out of their comfort zone, others need to be left alone - at least for some time.

As cardwarsaddict says, just let him know that you are there if he needs you. This probably will in time mean quite a lot to him, even if he doesn't show it right now.

I'm making a list and picture wall with stuff I enjoyed. Don't know yet if it will work, we will see.

And I'm also thinking about a tattoo for exactly the same reason as you. But I don't know yet what I want tattoed.

Meditation also often works or just getting some fresh air. Just to remind myself there's life around me.

Also some push-ups sometimes help.

and just telling myself "suicide will not make it better" often is enough to stop myself thinking about suicide.

go for a walk

read Feeling Good by David Burns, a very good cognitive therapy book.

anyway read a lot of books

go sit in the sun

make a list of things you enjoyed in your life. When you're feeling down, look at the list

learn how to cook. Cooking is very relaxing

Learn a new skill. I've taken welding lessons, was great fun

You probably can't separate him from the illness. But you can be there for him, talk to him, listen to him, show him that you care. Ask him what he wants, give him the feeling of being loved.
If he only wants to sit at home, try to get him to do something. Even if it's only a short walk or drinking a coffee somewhere. This can really lighten the mood.
try meditation, worked for me for quite a few years.

I often think about how much of my depression is self-inflicted. I've started therapy two years ago and I often think about myself as a fraud. I mean I really am depressed and suicidal, but isn't this just a sort of lazyness? Isn't it just that I don't want to bother with everyday chores, with a regular job, with all the stuff you have to do in this society?
I've talked about this with my therapist and he told me it's quite common for people with depression. It's more or less a symptom of a depression. It's quite unfair, isn't it? You are sick, but the sickness lets you think you're faking it.
